ambiguous.item: A code generated by an authenticator app on your phone
ambiguous.why: Doctrinally the factor is the possessed device/seeded token app, so it is 'something you have'. A practitioner could argue the user actually presents a transient value they read and type, which behaves like a one-time shared secret ('something you know'). ISC2 CC resolves this as possession because the secret is bound to the enrolled device, not to memory.

ambiguous.item: Your date of birth, used as a verification question
ambiguous.why: Knowledge-based verification questions are classed as 'something you know', even though the underlying fact is weak and widely discoverable. A practitioner could defensibly call a date of birth an inherent, immutable attribute of the person ('something you are' / an identity attribute rather than a secret), which is why many frameworks disallow it as an authentication factor at all.

ambiguous.item: A peer offers to sell you leaked ISC2 exam questions, and you decline and report it
ambiguous.my_answer: Canon IV — advance and protect the profession
ambiguous.alternative: Canon II — act honourably, honestly, justly, responsibly and legally
ambiguous.why: Exam-integrity breaches devalue the credential itself, which is the classic Canon IV 'protect the profession' case. But trafficking in stolen exam content is also theft of intellectual property and a breach of the candidate agreement, so refusing it is defensibly plain honesty and legality under Canon II.

ambiguous.item: You decline to exaggerate a threat in a sales pitch to frighten a prospect into buying
ambiguous.my_answer: Canon II — act honourably, honestly, justly, responsibly and legally
ambiguous.alternative: Canon IV — advance and protect the profession
ambiguous.why: Misrepresenting risk to close a sale is dishonest dealing, squarely Canon II. A practitioner could argue FUD-based selling is exactly the conduct that erodes public trust in security professionals generally, making it a Canon IV 'protect the profession' matter.

ambiguous.item: A client pressures you to overstate their security posture in an audit report, and you refuse
ambiguous.my_answer: Canon II — act honourably, honestly, justly, responsibly and legally
ambiguous.alternative: Canon III — provide diligent and competent service to principals
ambiguous.why: Refusing to falsify findings is honesty under Canon II. However, the counterparty is the principal, and Canon III's duty of diligent service includes not subordinating professional judgement to a client's wishes; a third reading is Canon I, since a false attestation relied on by others harms public trust.

ambiguous.item: You tell a client up front that a specialised cloud engagement is beyond what you are qualified to deliver
ambiguous.my_answer: Canon III — provide diligent and competent service to principals
ambiguous.alternative: Canon II — act honourably, honestly, justly, responsibly and legally
ambiguous.why: Declining work outside your competence is the textbook Canon III duty to serve principals competently and only in areas of qualification. It is equally defensible as Canon II, since the act itself is an honest disclosure of your own limits rather than a service-delivery decision.
